{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-tn","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"a7ed44390cd08a234f3391bfb91084f02d6239f2abf2c9f53ef983fa66886f2f","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-tn-class-d:lineage:50","source_registry_sha256":"8b0b6a068a0aa720d419171b5007a2610ed6c5012eeff522b57713cf9226eb71","source_liveness_sha256":"d27b9a94f03ec29d960b8eea38966606a7d3fdb703ad30b19ecd93f9bc70d0c7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Alcohol, other drugs and driving","heading":"C — Alcohol, other drugs and driving: how alcohol works in the body, blood alcohol concentration, crash risk, effects on judgment, vision and reaction, everyday drugs, the DUI law, implied consent, DUI penalties and the under-21 laws","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Alcohol, other drugs and driving: how alcohol works in the body, blood alcohol concentration, crash risk, effects on judgment, vision and reaction, everyday drugs, the DUI law, implied consent, DUI penalties and the under-21 laws
Knowledge domain: what Tennessee drivers must know about alcohol and other drugs — how the body absorbs and clears alcohol, what blood alcohol concentration means and what raises it, how impairment multiplies crash risk, how alcohol damages judgment, vision, reaction and alertness, why ordinary medicines can impair, what the DUI and implied consent laws say, what a conviction costs, and the special laws for drivers under twenty-one.

FACT_ID: sec12-F01 | anchor: A01
Tennessee law requires that no less than 25 percent of knowledge test questions deal with driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec12-F02 | anchor: A01
Researchers estimate that between 10:00 p.m. and 2:00 a.m., about 1 in every 10 drivers on the road is intoxicated. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec12-F03 | anchor: A01
Nearly 50 percent of drivers arrested for DUI are social or moderate drinkers rather than heavy drinkers. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec12-F04 | anchor: A01
Alcohol begins passing into the bloodstream within one to two minutes after you drink it. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec12-F05 | anchor: A01
You become intoxicated when you drink alcohol faster than your liver can oxidize it, and the higher the share of alcohol in your blood, the more intoxicated you are. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec12-F06 | anchor: A01
The liver can oxidize only about one drink per hour, and coffee, exercise or a cold shower cannot speed that up; only time sobers a drinker. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec12-F07 | anchor: A01
Blood alcohol concentration, or BAC, measures the percentage of alcohol in the blood, and the higher the number, the more impaired the person. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec12-F08 | anchor: A01
In Tennessee a BAC of .08 is the intoxication level that is always illegal, which equals eight drops of alcohol for every 10,000 drops of blood. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec12-F09 | anchor: A01
Your BAC depends on your body weight, how long you have been drinking and how much alcohol you have had. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec12-F10 | anchor: A01
Every drink taken within an hour pushes your BAC higher, whatever you weigh and whatever kind of alcoholic drink it is. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec12-F11 | anchor: A01
Three drinks in one hour affect you more than the same three drinks spread over three hours. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec12-F12 | anchor: A01
Because alcohol dissolves in water and not in fat, of two people with the same weight, the one with more body fat will show intoxication first. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec12-F13 | anchor: A01
Food in the stomach slows how fast alcohol is absorbed, but all of the alcohol still reaches the blood eventually. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec12-F14 | anchor: A01
Compared with a sober driver, a driver at .10 BAC is seven times more likely to cause a crash, at .15 about 25 times, and at .17 about 50 times. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec12-F15 | anchor: A02
Every person at a .10 BAC is too impaired to drive safely, and driving skill, judgment and vision are greatly impaired at levels as low as .03 and .04, especially in young drinkers. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec12-F16 | anchor: A02
Judgment and vision are the two abilities most important to driving, and small amounts of alcohol affect both. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec12-F17 | anchor: A02
Your ability to judge speed, time and distance changes after only one drink. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec12-F18 | anchor: A02
Alcohol-impaired judgment shows up as needless risks such as speeding, passing without enough clear distance, rushing around curves and showing off. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec12-F19 | anchor: A02
Alcohol cuts your ability to see clearly at night by more than half and slows your recovery from headlight glare. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec12-F20 | anchor: A02
At a .05 BAC, your side vision shrinks by about 30 percent. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec12-F21 | anchor: A02
Reaction time and coordination start to suffer at a BAC as low as .02. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec12-F22 | anchor: A03
Alcohol in any amount is a depressant, not a stimulant; the lift people feel from small doses comes from lowered inhibitions. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec12-F23 | anchor: A03
When alcohol is combined with another depressant such as a tranquilizer or sedative, the effects multiply rather than simply add together. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec12-F24 | anchor: A03
Having a prescription for a drug is no legal defense for driving under its influence. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec12-F25 | anchor: A03
Over-the-counter cold tablets, cough syrups and allergy remedies can contain antihistamines, alcohol or codeine, so read the label warnings before driving. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec12-F26 | anchor: A03
In Tennessee it is illegal to drive or be in physical control of a motor vehicle on a public road or in a place open to the public, such as a shopping center or apartment complex, while under the influence of any intoxicant, marijuana, narcotic or stimulant drug. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec12-F27 | anchor: A03
It is also illegal in Tennessee to drive or be in physical control of a vehicle when your blood or breath alcohol concentration is .08 percent or higher. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec12-F28 | anchor: A03
A BAC under .08 does not clear you of DUI, and a driver can even be convicted with a BAC of .00 if drugs impaired the driving. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec12-F29 | anchor: A03
Under the Implied Consent Law, driving in Tennessee means you have agreed to be tested for alcohol or drugs in your blood when an officer with reasonable grounds asks. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec12-F30 | anchor: A03
If you are arrested and refuse the test an officer requests, the court will likely suspend your driving privileges for 12 months. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec12-F31 | anchor: A03
Tennessee's No Refusal law, passed in 2012, lets officers seek search warrants for blood samples from suspected impaired drivers. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec12-F32 | anchor: A03
DUI penalties are the same whether the driver used alcohol or drugs, including prescription and over-the-counter drugs. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec12-F33 | anchor: A03
Any DUI conviction requires, as a probation condition, picking up litter for three 8-hour shifts while wearing clothing that says I am a DRUNK DRIVER. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec12-F34 | anchor: A04
Driving under the influence with a child under 18 in the vehicle adds a mandatory minimum of 30 days in jail and a mandatory minimum $1,000 fine on top of other penalties. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec12-F35 | anchor: A04
A driver under the influence who causes a crash that kills someone may be charged with vehicular homicide, and one that injures someone may bring an aggravated assault charge. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec12-F36 | anchor: A04
A driver's vehicle will be seized after two DUI convictions within five years when both events happened after January 1997. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec12-F37 | anchor: A04
A person with 2 DUIs within a five-year period must drive a vehicle with an ignition interlock device, which keeps the car from starting when the driver's BAC is too high, for six months after reinstatement. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec12-F38 | anchor: A05
If you are 18, 19 or 20 and are convicted of buying, trying to buy or possessing alcohol, you lose your driving privilege for one year, or two years for a second offense, even if no vehicle was involved. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec12-F39 | anchor: A05
A person aged 13 to 17 found to have possessed, consumed or sold alcohol or drugs loses driving privileges for one year or until turning 17, whichever period runs longer, even without ever having held a license. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec12-F40 | anchor: A05
A driver aged 16 to 20 found driving with a .02 BAC or under the influence of alcohol or another intoxicant is convicted of underage driving while impaired, with a one-year license loss and a $250 fine. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec12-F41 | anchor: A05
Young drivers have a much higher crash risk than older drivers at BAC levels from .01 to .08, because of low alcohol tolerance and limited driving experience. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec12-F42 | anchor: A05
A 12-ounce bottle of beer holds about as much alcohol as a 1-ounce shot of whiskey. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec12-F43 | anchor: A05
It takes about one hour to cancel the effects of one drink and about three hours for three drinks. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0097]

Misconceptions: coffee, cold showers and exercise do not sober you up, only time does; alcohol is a depressant, not a stimulant; a BAC under the legal limit does not protect you from a DUI charge; a prescription is no defense; beer is not weaker than a shot of liquor in a standard serving; drug DUIs are not punished more lightly than alcohol DUIs.
Mnemonics: one drink, one hour; judgment goes first; same penalty for drugs and alcohol; no thanks, I am driving.
Glossary: BAC means blood alcohol concentration, the percentage of alcohol in the blood; implied consent means agreeing to a blood or breath test by choosing to drive in Tennessee; depressant means a substance that slows nerve impulses and body functions; ignition interlock means a device that blocks the engine from starting if the driver's BAC is too high.
Dynamic facts: DUI fines, jail terms, revocation periods, the refusal suspension, interlock rules and the under-twenty-one penalties are set by Tennessee law and can change; confirm them on official Tennessee sources before showing them to learners.
